moduleTitle: Rites of passage in Christian life

note.specFocus: Baptism, confirmation and other key rites of passage that mark stages of Christian life.
note.sourcePages: Written to match the Edexcel specification; no supplied booklet for this subject.
note.summary:
3.3 Rites of Passage in Christian Life
Rites of passage mark important transitions in a Christian's life and relationship with the Church.
Baptism
• Infant baptism (common in Catholic, Orthodox and many Protestant churches): a baby is baptised with water, often poured over the head, while godparents and parents make promises on the child's behalf to raise them in the Christian faith.
• Believer's baptism (practised by Baptists and some others): a person old enough to personally profess faith is fully immersed in water, symbolising dying to an old life and rising to new life in Christ (Romans 6:4).
• The two approaches reflect a genuine denominational disagreement: whether baptism should respond to personal, conscious faith, or whether it can express God's grace reaching a child before they can respond, similar to circumcision in the Old Testament covenant.
Confirmation
• Allows someone baptised as an infant to personally confirm the promises made on their behalf, taking on the faith as their own choice.
• In Catholic and Orthodox traditions, a bishop lays hands on and anoints the candidate with chrism oil, understood to strengthen them with the Holy Spirit (echoing Pentecost, Acts 2).
• Often marks full, mature membership of the Church, including full participation in receiving the Eucharist.
Other rites of passage
• Marriage and funeral services are also key Christian rites of passage, marking the formation of a new family and the committal of the deceased to God's care with the hope of resurrection.
Exam link: when asked to "Discuss whether baptism should only be performed on believing adults", name the Baptist position explicitly and contrast it with infant baptism traditions, rather than discussing baptism in general.

questions.modelAnswer:
A strong response develops two separate points:

1. In infant baptism, common in Catholic, Orthodox and many Protestant churches, a baby is baptised with water, often poured over the head, while godparents and parents make promises on the child's behalf to raise them in the Christian faith.

2. In believer's baptism, practised by Baptists and some other denominations, a person who is old enough to personally profess faith is fully immersed in water, symbolising dying to their old life and rising to new life in Christ (Romans 6:4).
questions.question: Outline two features of a Christian baptism.

questions.examTip: For 6 marks, combine accurate knowledge with explanation. Explain why each point matters and link it directly to the question; avoid simply listing facts.
questions.modelAnswer:
A developed answer could explain the issue through three connected points.

First, Confirmation allows a person who was baptised as an infant to personally confirm the promises that were made on their behalf by parents and godparents, taking on the Christian faith as their own choice rather than one made for them.

Second, In the Catholic and Orthodox traditions, confirmation is understood as a sacrament in which the Holy Spirit strengthens the believer, often with the bishop laying hands on and anointing the candidate with oil (chrism), echoing the gifts of the Holy Spirit at Pentecost (Acts 2).

Finally, Confirmation is often seen as a significant milestone marking the transition to full, mature membership of the church community, after which a person can fully participate in receiving the Eucharist in many traditions.
questions.question: Explain why confirmation is important for many Christians.

questions.examTip: For a 10-mark discussion, analyse different aspects of the Christian issue and how they interrelate. Finish with a reasoned conclusion; do not just list advantages and disadvantages.
questions.modelAnswer:
A FIRST PERSPECTIVE

One line of reasoning is: Baptists and some other denominations argue that baptism should follow a personal, conscious profession of faith, since the New Testament examples of baptism, such as the Ethiopian official in Acts 8:36–38, show adults choosing baptism for themselves after believing.

A second consideration is: Believer's baptism, they argue, better reflects the meaning of baptism as a response to and public declaration of one's own faith, rather than a decision made by parents on a child's behalf before the child can understand it.

AN ALTERNATIVE PERSPECTIVE

A different perspective is: Most Catholic, Orthodox and many other Protestant churches baptise infants, arguing this reflects God's grace reaching out to a person before they can respond, similar to how children were included in the Old Testament covenant through circumcision, and relies on parents and godparents to nurture the child's faith until confirmation.

A further consideration is: Infant baptism also welcomes a child fully into the church community and family of faith from the very beginning of life, which these traditions see as a gift rather than something that should wait until later understanding is possible.

JUDGEMENT

Overall, the conclusion should weigh the arguments above against this key consideration: this is a genuine and long-standing denominational disagreement, with Baptist traditions emphasising the necessity of personal, believing faith at baptism, and other major traditions emphasising God's grace and the inclusion of children within the believing community from birth. It should then state which perspective is more convincing in relation to the exact wording of the question and explain why, rather than assuming that every Christian will reach the same view.
questions.question: Discuss whether baptism should only be performed on believing adults.

questions.examTip: Use accurate Christian teaching, explain why each point matters, and in an evaluation compare arguments before reaching a reasoned conclusion.
questions.modelAnswer:
A FIRST PERSPECTIVE
Teaching gives coherent meaning to the themes of infant and believer's baptism, confirmation, commitment, cleansing and entry into community and helps Christians decide what is true.

AN ALTERNATIVE PERSPECTIVE
Practice makes belief visible in worship, compassion, family and service; without action faith may be empty. Christians within different traditions may also disagree about how the teaching should be lived.

JUDGEMENT
A reasoned conclusion should compare the authority and practical effect of belief and action, acknowledge diversity, and decide which is more persuasive for the exact claim.
